criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and urban population access to water supply and sanitation (sewerage) services in Brazil from the nineteenth century to the 2010s.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper clearly examines institutional, legal, regulatory, and governance factors (public vs. private utility management models, municipal autarquias, state-owned sanitation companies, Concessions Law no. 8987 of 1995, Law 11.445 of 2007, mixed-capital shareholding, and PPPs). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, utility ownership and concession structures directly governing service access are within the protocol's rule-type mechanism scope insofar as the paper compares public, municipal, state, and private utility ownership models against household connection coverage, although much of the historical narrative discusses broad macro-sector policy shifts without analysing a specific operational rule-type mechanism empirically. Regardless, the paper is excluded under both readings because it fails Criterion 3 (no empirical method or primary data).
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative historical and policy overview with no primary data, no empirical methodology or data/methods section, and no systematic review protocol. While the paper reproduces descriptive regional cross-tabulations of secondary IBGE survey and census data (Tables 2-5, Figure 1) and narratively cites four prior Brazilian empirical studies (Heller et al., 2006; Rezende et al., 2007; Heller et al., 2009; Ohira, 2005), it conducts no identifiable empirical analysis or systematic synthesis -> exclude as E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports secondary descriptive statistics on the proportion of urban households/population with house connections to water supply and sewerage systems across regions and management models (Figure 1, Tables 3 and 5).
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, analytical methodology, sample sizes/denominators, and data-linkage procedures explaining how municipality-level management classifications from the 2008 IBGE sanitation survey were combined with 2010 census urban connection figures.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper seeks to contribute to the current debate, showing from the historical record of how access to services has improved, in both quantity and quality, and from the current shortfall, how the institutional models adopted at different times and in different parts of the country can help to explain the sector’s past performance and suggest future directions.
Within each category of management model and each region of Brazil, Table 3 shows the proportion of households with access to full house water connections and internal plumbing.
Some studies have sought to compare the outcomes from the use of different institutional models for the provision of WSS in Brazil.

New forms of participation of private capital in service provision have also appeared, such as the increase in private shareholding capital in some of the major state water companies, which were previously in entirely public ownership

This paper has shown how the Brazilian government’s policy with regard to the management of water and sanitation services has oscillated in accordance with historical trends in the sector, swinging between state and municipal, and between public and private.

raw_response.exposure: Institutional ownership and management models for water supply and sanitation (direct municipal public administration, municipally owned enterprise/autarquia, state-owned sanitation company, private concessionaire, mixed-capital shareholding, and public-private partnerships)
raw_response.outcome: Proportion of urban households/population with house connections to water supply and sewerage networks (descriptive secondary figures from IBGE surveys and census)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Municipalities and urban population/households in Brazil (secondary IBGE aggregates cited without sample sizes or empirical methodology)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Heller, Rezende, and Cairncross (2014) is a narrative historical and policy overview of public, municipal, state-owned, and private management models in Brazil's water supply and sanitation sector from the nineteenth century to the early 2010s. Although the article addresses water and sanitation access (c1) and utility ownership/concession arrangements (c2) and includes illustrative summary tables from published IBGE surveys/census reports alongside narrative mentions of four prior empirical studies, it has no primary data, no empirical methodology or analytical study design, no sample sizes/denominators, and no systematic synthesis protocol. Both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type decision and the plain Criterion 2 decision are exclude (E05).
raw_response.study_design: Historical and policy overview (narrative overview with descriptive secondary official statistics; no empirical study design)
